The four stranded gRPC-Go members are BENIGN. The gRPC archive keeps the supplied MALICIOUS conviction without rejudgment. Grype 0.112.0, Linux x86-64 conda build h643be8f_0, is BENIGN. No specimen, installed CLI, network payload, or destructive fixture was executed.

All 802 files in the gRPC archive are byte-identical, by relative member name and content, to google.golang.org/grpc v1.57.0. Forager fetched that exact module and verified its module sum against sum.golang.org. This comparison corroborates individual code tracing; it does not supply the reason for the archive conviction or establish any deployment context.

* `end2end_test.go` creates test RPC services, binds ephemeral localhost TCP listeners or temporary Unix sockets, chooses fixture TLS keys or explicit insecure credentials, invokes unary/streaming RPCs, and checks metadata, deadlines, framing, compression and shutdown. The Unix unlink removes its test socket. `InsecureSkipVerify` wraps the test connection in `withServerTester`; it is retained as an accurate notable capability.
* `balancer_test.go` registers test balancers and a manual resolver, establishes fixture TLS credentials, configures routing, passes metadata and tests picks, loads, connection state and producer lifetimes. Its initializer registers a test load parser. These are ordinary test effects, independently supported by this member's source.
* `goaway_test.go` creates local servers and clients, configures maximum connection age and keepalive enforcement, holds RPC streams open, calls graceful shutdown and verifies GOAWAY/PING behavior. Timing, sockets and goroutines implement the protocol tests rather than a command channel or denial-of-service payload.
* `xds_resolver_test.go` installs/restores a fake xDS client constructor, creates a local management server, builds resolver bootstrap configurations, feeds listener/route updates through callbacks and checks service configurations and selection results. XXHash hashes routing keys. Its outgoing metadata is attached to RPC contexts. The test callbacks are not covert remote execution.

Grype's conda payload has exactly one installed member, `bin/grype` (129,364,201 bytes). Its SHA-256, 931ad0fe4295475de117f72f34ceb9fad33816fd51a89afd16638719b2ab412b, agrees with `info/paths.json`. Other members are package metadata, recipes, licenses and vendored reference source. The recipe sets the CLI version through Go link flags; there is no installed post-link script. The fetched Grype v0.112.0 source archive matches the recipe's SHA-256, 0e158ac297c79a132c3d5960fe13995ecb38a7f9fc81402d8102c220600d3de8. This verifies the reference source, not whole-binary reproducibility.

The ELF is a Go PIE with symbols and debug information. Targeted Rizin disassembly, annotated from 120,692 ELF symbols, confirms `main.main` at 0x275f160 calls `cli.create` at 0x275d9a0, which installs the root, database and other CLI commands. `commands.runGrype` at 0x2731100 constructs the result writer and calls vulnerability matching. Its closure at 0x2733020 calls `LoadVulnerabilityDB`; the closure at 0x2732aa0 calls `getProviderConfig` and `pkg.Provide`. Source tracing follows the selected input through package cataloging, matching and result formatting. Registry authentication, filesystem walking, decompression, TLS, hashing, temporary files and child execution fit these functions. The `libphp` bytes establish a module-name reference, without establishing PHP implementation or loading; Semgrep is invoked by a vendored CI workflow. Neither makes the Grype executable PHP or Semgrep. Packaging and these execution paths tip the benign judgment; no host deployment context was supplied.

Seven new notable capabilities cover gRPC header setting/sending, trailers, outgoing metadata, default service configuration, constructor-linked graceful shutdown, and an actual Semgrep command in a workflow run field. The shutdown rule follows the receiver to the canonical grpc constructor and accepts an aliased import. Quoted calls and unrelated receivers do not match. The former bare Semgrep word matched labels, strings and workflow mentions while living under tool identity; it is replaced by the supported workflow invocation. Explicit SAST integration retains that operation, while two JavaScript exclusions now require actual Semgrep rule-fixture context instead of a bare word.

The libphp matcher is relocated unchanged to library-path references; its Apache/PHP memory-hook consumer follows the new ID. The YAML rule-list matcher is relocated unchanged to pattern-catalog metadata, with its exact pipeline exclusion updated. This observation claims a list with pattern/match/severity fields, not a particular scanner's identity or use of its entries. Ancestor identity selectors intentionally no longer receive those neutral facts: an arbitrary module name or rule table cannot establish a trusted product. Exact consumers and ancestor selectors were inspected before these moves. There were no existing focused libphp positive fixtures; native compiled name/near-miss controls and the actual Grype binary check the retained matcher. The fixture binaries are compiled temporarily and only scanned.

The Go dial grouping is raised to notable, and the private/key-named PEM path observation is raised from component to notable with a description that does not assert the file's contents. Matchers and scope are unchanged. The engine filters the now-notable pure-any dial group from output as redundant, and its enclosing dial rollup is consequently absent from archive output. The underlying dial API atoms remain, the grouping still resolves during evaluation, and the hostile Go reverse-shell consumer passes before and after. No accurate attack observation was lost. Generic Semgrep name-only identities are intentionally no longer reported; the supplied workflow retains the actual command behavior.

The supplied gRPC archive conviction remains inconsistent with the local classifier. Three to five hostile traits cannot be supported by these upstream-identical bytes: no concealed staging, unauthorized command channel, exfiltration, persistence or destructive payload was found. Networking, TLS, codecs, execution and test effects remain covered at their supported severities. The archive conviction's underlying evidence was not provided; arbitrary hostile rules would not repair that evidence gap.

`review.json` records each sample, marker note, SHA, counts, probabilities and every changed archive analysis unit. No units disappear: 777 gRPC analysis units and 1,354 Grype units are compared. Initial cached archive results differed from current analyzer output, so the controlled comparisons use fresh analysis. Paired Grype scans use the same 30-second Rizin subprocess budget; large-binary control-flow recovery remains incomplete, independently supplemented by direct native disassembly. Atomscan also reports its older v18 model feature specification against the engine's expected v21. These limits do not establish benign intent or successful runtime execution.

Run `python3 testdata/stranded-grpc-grype-review/check.py`: 63 assertions cover calls versus quoted examples, unrelated receiver decoys, aliased imports, literal module names versus near misses, workflow commands versus labels, catalog schema, severity, and the existing hostile reverse-shell consumer. The existing stranded-standard-components suite also passes its 12 controls. The older oct24 wrapper scans its own check.py and fails a blanket substring assertion on its own literal `validation failed`; replaying its 22 cases with explicitly selected targets passes all 43 behavioral assertions. Full scans/facts, disassembly, provenance, baseline rules and test logs remain in scratch/stranded-current.

`marker-notes.txt` contains the exact one-line notes for copying verbatim into a commit body. The two archive/package markers use their listed sample paths; the four member markers are beside their extracted Go files.
